q: The best Instagram alternatives for artists
title: Best Instagram alternatives for artists
description: A fair look at Cara, Bluesky, Pixelfed, ArtStation, Behance and Emera: what each does well, who runs it and how they treat AI.
short: The best Instagram alternative for artists depends on what you need: Cara is a live artist community with AI filtering, Bluesky has open feeds, Pixelfed is open source with chronological timelines, and Emera is a new nonprofit network with signed posts. Here is how they compare.

sections.h: What artists usually want from an alternative
sections.html:
Most artists who look for a new home want the same few things: a place where the work is the star, a clear stance on generative AI, a feed that is not a mystery, and some control over their own account. The options below answer those in different ways, and none is the single right pick for everyone.

We built Emera, so we are listed here too. We have tried to describe every option the way its own site and docs describe it, and to say plainly where another option is the better fit today.

Cara is an app and website made for artists, run by founder Jingna Zhang with a group of volunteers. Its listing says an AI detector filters AI images out of user portfolios, and it applies NoAI tags to art as a signal to scrapers. You can customize your home feed and set up custom Explore tabs, and it has portfolio features and job listings. The iOS app is free with optional tips and supporter tiers.

If your main concern is an art community that keeps AI-generated images out, Cara is built around exactly that. For details on its source code, account export and company structure, confirm on cara.app, since we could not read those from its own pages.

Bluesky is run by Bluesky Social, a public benefit corporation, and the app's source code is published under the MIT license. Its FAQ says you can pick from over 40,000 feeds, switch servers without losing your username, followers or posts, and sign up without an invite. Bluesky has said it does not use user content to train generative AI. It is available on web, iOS and Android.

Bluesky is a general network rather than an art-first one, but apps built for it, such as Flashes, give it a photo-and-video look. Flashes is a native Bluesky photo and video app from Birdsong Apps GmbH.

Pixelfed is a photo-sharing platform released under the AGPL-3.0 license. It uses the ActivityPub protocol, so it connects with Mastodon and other fediverse apps, and its timelines are chronological with no content-ranking algorithm. Official and third-party apps exist for iOS and Android. Each Pixelfed server is run by its own community, so the rules and moderation depend on where you sign up.

ArtStation and Behance are portfolio sites that many artists already use for hiring and showcases, not social feeds in the Instagram sense. ArtStation has added AI declarations and filters so visitors can hide AI-generated work. For Behance's current AI and training settings, confirm on behance.net.

Emera is an open-source, nonprofit network with its own accounts. Every post carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up, and people are marked while automated accounts are labeled as automated. If you find a copy of your work elsewhere, you report it and Emera helps you file the takedown, with every step on your dashboard. You own your account and can export everything you made and your follower list any time, and posts show a 'Why you are seeing this' reason.

Emera is new. If you need a large community today, the other options here are further along.

Bluesky is live with working apps on web, iOS and Android, over 40,000 feeds and a pledge not to train generative AI on user content.

faqs.a: It depends on what matters most to you. Cara is built for artists and filters AI images. Bluesky has open feeds. Pixelfed is open source with chronological timelines. Emera is a new nonprofit network that signs every post with who shared it and when.
Pixelfed is released under AGPL-3.0 and Bluesky's app source code is under the MIT license. Emera's code is open source too. For Cara, confirm on cara.app.

faqs.a: On Emera you can export everything you made and your follower list any time. On Bluesky, check its help center for how moving works. Pixelfed is part of the fediverse, so check pixelfed.org for how moving works on your server.

faqs.a: Bluesky has said it does not use user content to train generative AI. Cara filters AI-generated images and tags art with NoAI. Read each platform's terms before you upload, since they can change.

title: Open source Instagram alternatives
description: Pixelfed, Bluesky photo apps and Emera compared: licenses, who runs them, how feeds work and how feeds work.
short: The open source Instagram alternatives are Pixelfed (AGPL-3.0, fediverse, chronological timelines), Bluesky and the photo apps built for it such as Flashes (MIT-licensed Bluesky app), and Emera (open-source code, nonprofit, signed posts). Here is what each is like to use.

sections.html: For a social app, open source can mean three different things: the app's code is public, the server's code is public, or the protocol underneath is an open standard anyone can build on. It helps to know which one you are getting, because it decides how much you can move, inspect and self-host.

Pixelfed is a photo-sharing platform released under the AGPL-3.0 license. Its repository describes it as photo sharing for everyone, without algorithmic gatekeeping. It speaks ActivityPub, so you can follow and be followed across Mastodon and other fediverse apps. Timelines are chronological, with Local, Global and Home feeds. Official apps for iOS and Android launched in January 2025, and third-party apps exist too.

Because Pixelfed is federated, anyone can run a server, and each server sets its own rules. That is the strength of it and also the thing to check before you sign up.

sections.h: Bluesky and photo apps built for it
sections.html:
Bluesky's app source is published under the MIT license. Bluesky's FAQ says you can change servers without losing your username, friends or posts. Anyone can build a feed, and its FAQ says there are over 40,000 to choose from.

Flashes, from Birdsong Apps GmbH, is a native Bluesky photo and video app for Apple devices with photo filters and portfolio building. We did not find a published Flashes codebase, so treat it as an app for Bluesky rather than an open-source app.

Emera is a nonprofit network with open-source code. Each post carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up, people are marked while automated accounts are labeled as automated, and reposts point back to the original post. You can pick feeds, and posts show a 'Why you are seeing this' reason. You own your account and can export everything you made and your follower list any time.

Emera is new, so it has a small footprint compared with the options above.

title: Emera vs Cara: which fits your art?
description: Cara is a live artist community with AI filtering; Emera is a new nonprofit network with signed posts. How they differ and who each suits.
short: Cara is a live, artist-focused app with AI filtering and portfolio features; Emera is a new, open-source nonprofit network where every post carries a signed record of who shared it and when. Choose Cara for an art community today, Emera for provenance and account portability.

sections.html:
Cara is an image-sharing app and website for artists, created by Jingna Zhang, who runs it with a group of volunteers. It grew out of artists' concern about AI-generated art on larger platforms. Its App Store listing says an AI detector filters AI images out of portfolios, and it also applies NoAI tags to art as a voluntary signal to AI scrapers.

Day to day it works as both a portfolio and a feed. You can customize your home feed, set up custom Explore tabs, share images, GIFs and embedded videos, use direct messages and bookmarks, and browse job listings. The iOS app is free, with optional tips and supporter tiers from the developer, Cara Project, Inc.

Emera is an open-source nonprofit network for everyone who makes things. Every post carries a signed record (C2PA content credentials) of who shared it and when it went up, and a Signed badge says exactly what was checked and nothing more. People are marked, and automated accounts are labeled as automated. Reposts point back to the original post.

Found a copy of your work elsewhere? You report it, Emera helps you file the takedown, and every step shows on your dashboard. You own your account, and you can export everything you made and your follower list any time.

If you want an art community you can join today, with an AI-image filter and a portfolio built in, Cara is the stronger fit. If you care about a signed record on each post, takedown help for copies, and an account you can export in full, Emera is built around those. Many artists will reasonably have a profile on both.

Emera is new. We do not describe it as bigger or more established than Cara, because it is not.

If you find a copy of your work elsewhere, you report it and Emera helps you file the takedown, with every step on your dashboard. Many people will use both: Bluesky for its established network today, Emera for signed posts and takedown help.

title: Pixsy alternative: Emera Protect compared
description: Pixsy and Emera Protect side by side: what each watches, plan prices, who files takedowns and what you keep from a recovery.
short: Pixsy is an established image-monitoring service with a free plan, paid plans from $19 a month and a 50% share of what it recovers. Emera Protect covers videos, music, photos and art, starts with a free report, costs $10 or $100 a month, and you keep 70% of recoveries. Here is where each fits.

sections.html: Pixsy scans the public web for copies of your images and emails you when it finds matches, according to its pricing page. Its free plan monitors 500 images and accepts unlimited case submissions but includes no takedown notices. Paid Monitor plans run from $19 a month (2,000 images, 20 takedowns a month) to $89 a month (100,000 images, 900 takedowns), with business pricing on request. On recoveries it takes 50% of the compensation it collects and charges nothing if it recovers nothing. Cases that need legal action go to partner law firms; Pixsy lists 30.

Emera Protect finds copies and fake accounts, files the takedowns and tracks each one to a Removed receipt. The Creator plan is $10 a month and watches up to 100 posts weekly across videos, music, photos, art and designs on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and the web. Pro is $100 a month with unlimited posts checked daily, fake accounts using your name or face and automatic filing. Enterprise is custom. For money, Get paid sends a claim letter and partner US copyright lawyers sue if the copier does not pay; it is no win, no fee and you keep 70%. US cases come first.

If your work is mostly still images and you want the longest-running tool with many import sources and takedowns in many countries, Pixsy is built for that. If you make videos, music or mixed work, want the report for free, or want the larger share of a recovery, Emera Protect is built for that. You do not have to pick for life: both let you submit a case without committing to a paid plan. Whatever you use, registering your work early decides what a US court can award (statutory damages).
